> 「随说是经，乃至四句偈等，当知此处，一切世间天、人、阿修罗，皆应供养，如佛塔庙。……若是经典所在之处，即为有佛。」

The twelfth section makes a claim about places: wherever this sutra is taught, even four lines of it, that spot is to be honoured as a stupa is honoured — and where the sutra is, there is a buddha.

The claim has been used for two opposite purposes ever since. One is to build shrines and sell indulgences. The other is to dismiss all reverence as superstition.

The section supports neither.

## 随说 is about not choosing the venue

随, "following along with" — wherever, with whoever, as conditions allow. No preferred hall, no curated audience.

This is the same move as the begging bowl in section one. The teaching does not require a purified location. It requires a place where someone is actually speaking and someone is actually listening, which is a rarer thing than either a hall or a book.

## 供养 is not a transaction

Offering flowers, incense, reverence, support — the book's definition is that this is the outward form of inward respect, and its function is to gather the mind.

Which is why the section's language is about honour, not about exchange. The moment the bow becomes a purchase — I give reverence, therefore something comes back — the act has changed category, and the object of reverence has become a vendor.

## 经典所在之处，即为有佛

Read as bibliolatry, this says a printed object contains a buddha. Read correctly, it says: where the meaning of this text is being carried and received, that is where the Tathāgata appears.

The distinction decides an ordinary question. Is it superstition to keep a copy of a sutra on a clean shelf and bow to it? Not necessarily. Is it superstition to believe the paper is the thing? Yes — and the same correction applies to statues, reliquaries, and every object in every tradition.

The book's line: a signpost points at the destination; the signpost is not the destination. That does not make the signpost worthless. It makes it usable.

## 破执 is not 放逸

The common overcorrection: since marks are not to be grasped, reverence can be dropped, texts can be treated carelessly, forms can be discarded.

The section does not say this, and the book is emphatic: reverence is a means of taming the mind. What is rejected is the belief that this particular form *is* the sacred thing, or that it has powers to trade with. What is not rejected is respect, which is a working part of practice.

Discarding the form while keeping no respect is not freedom. It is just coarseness with a theory attached.

## 最上第一希有之法

The person who receives and holds this is said to accomplish the most rare dharma in the world.

Note what is not said: that this person has become a buddha, or reached a rank. What is rare is that someone, in a world habituated to grasping, is willing to hold a teaching whose entire content is *do not grasp*. Rarity is a statement about the availability of the view, not about the status of the holder.

## The test

Find the place where you keep something sacred. A book, an object, a photograph, a room.

Ask: do I honour this, or do I trade with it? The two are easy to confuse, because both involve care.

Honour leaves you lighter after the bow. Trade leaves you waiting.
